The BIS just published a pretty interesting paper on putting official government data on a blockchain.

Basically, they take things like GDP and inflation data, create cryptographic fingerprints of the data, combine them into a Merkle tree, and then record the final proof on the XRP Ledger.

That gives you a permanent, timestamped way to verify:

“Did this data actually come from the official source, and has anyone changed it?”

They also use Verifiable Credentials to tie the data back to the official publisher. The proof of concept was extremely fast too, roughly 3–5 seconds to publish and 1–2 seconds to verify.They chose XRPL for the prototype because of its fast finality and low fees. BUT here’s the part XRP maxis seem to be missing:

The BIS explicitly says the system is blockchain-agnostic. XRPL is the blockchain they used for the experiment. It doesn't mean XRPL is the required blockchain.

And the paper actually discusses the 2025 US Department of Commerce + Chainlink work, where Chainlink was used to bring GDP, PCE and other official economic data on-chain.

Basically there are two different layers:

BIS/XRPL:
Government data cryptographic proof blockchain verify authenticity

Chainlink:
Official data Chainlink infrastructure reliably deliver it to blockchains/apps

So no, this paper doesn't prove that XRPL replaces Chainlink. If anything, it shows why these systems can be complementary. The bigger takeaway is that blockchain is becoming a verification/trust layer for official data. XRPL was simply the blockchain used in this particular BIS prototype.

https://www.bis.org/publications/working-paper-1374-verifiable-official-statistics-blockchain-based-approach.pdf
